title: Supplementary Bibliometric and Public-Discourse Footprint
text:
Following the June 2026 global consensus terminology update, the current manuscript uses polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). This historical bibliometric and public-discourse analysis deliberately retains PCOS because it examines publications, indexing, quotations, and public discussion produced under that terminology; changing those source descriptions would obscure what was actually disseminated and searched.
This supplement describes the scholarly, extended-scholarly, grey-literature, and publicly visible web footprint of the 17 studies eligible for the systematic review. It was prepared to examine whether the frequently repeated claim that polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is associated with substantially lower resting energy expenditure (REE) can be linked to a distinctive pattern of dissemination around particular studies.
The analysis is descriptive. Citation and hyperlink counts do not establish that a paper caused a belief, and search-engine results do not provide an exhaustive census of public discussion. They can, however, establish whether a paper is relatively prominent, whether its numerical findings have travelled beyond academic articles, and how those findings are framed when they are repeated.

title: Supplementary Bibliometric and Public-Discourse Footprint
text:
Scholarly and extended-scholarly footprint
OpenAlex records were resolved by DOI and checked against title, author, and publication metadata. The snapshot was retrieved on 21 September 2026. openalex_citations is the number of works recorded by OpenAlex as citing the focal work. Lifetime citations per year were calculated from the OpenAlex first-publication date to the retrieval date. OpenAlex field-weighted citation impact (FWCI) and citation-normalised percentile are reported where available.
Citing works were grouped using the OpenAlex work-type classification. Journal articles and reviews were retained separately. Book chapters and books were treated as extended scholarly dissemination. Dissertations, preprints, paratexts, and residual non-journal records were grouped as grey literature for this descriptive audit. Because the work-level citation count and a live filtered query can differ slightly as the citation graph is recomputed, the report retains both the work-level count and the number of citing records that could be classified by type.

title: Supplementary Bibliometric and Public-Discourse Footprint
text:
Public web and social discussion
Targeted searches used each study’s exact title and DOI, supplemented for REE-focused studies by author-title combinations and distinctive numerical phrases. Reddit searches were restricted by domain and included the exact title, DOI, author name, and distinctive reported values where relevant. A source was counted only when the page itself could be verified as referring directly to the study through a link, title/author reference, or distinctive numerical signature. General statements about PCOS and metabolism without a traceable study reference were excluded.
The public-web counts are therefore conservative counts of verified pages found, not platform-wide totals. Deleted or private posts, unindexed pages, closed social networks, podcasts without transcripts, and link shorteners may be missed. Pages were also grouped into unique content items when an exact or explicitly documented relationship showed that one page was a repost or social share of another. All page URLs remain in the evidence table, but each grouped item contributes only once to the deduplicated totals.
Altmetric Details Pages were queried by DOI, or by PubMed ID when no DOI was available, on 22 September 2026. Attention Scores, last-mention dates, source counts, Dimensions citations, and Mendeley reader counts were transcribed from the free Details Pages. An exact-title search was used for the remaining record without a persistent identifier. A missing score was retained as missing: it indicates either that Altmetric explicitly reported no mentions or that the study could not be resolved, rather than a score of zero.
Altmetric source totals are platform-reported counts. They can represent users or source accounts rather than unique posts or pages and cannot be deduplicated against one another. They are therefore presented separately from the manually verified and deduplicated public-web audit.
The dated study snapshot, Altmetric snapshot, page-level evidence, and repost/share decisions are supplied in four pipeline-validated CSV files.

title: Supplementary Technical Analysis and Results
text:
This supplementary document provides the complete statistical model specifications, prior distributions, post-processing procedures, and full primary, sensitivity, and exploratory results supporting the main manuscript. It also records the updated literature search through September 2026 and the resulting study flow.
Following the June 2026 global consensus terminology update, this current supplementary analysis uses polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS; previously polycystic ovary syndrome, PCOS). PCOS is retained only where it describes the terminology used in the historical literature, source material, and database search strategy; the terminology update did not change the included data or analyses.

title: Supplementary Technical Analysis and Results
Supplementary Technical Analysis and Results
text:
Sensitivity analyses

Pairwise contrast based models
By way of pre-registered sensitivity analysis we also conducted pairwise contrast based models where we limited the included effects to those extracted from studies including only a directly comparable control and PMOS arm at baseline. These models were both as follows:
\[
\small
\begin{aligned}
\hat{\theta}_{ij} &\sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{ij}, \sigma^2_{ij}) \\[6pt]
\mu_{ij} &= \beta_0
       + \alpha_{0,\mathrm{lab}[i]}
       + \alpha_{0,\mathrm{study}[j]} \\[10pt]
\alpha_{0,\mathrm{lab}[i]} &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{0,\mathrm{lab}})
\text{, for lab i = 1,} \dots \text{,I} \\[12pt]
\alpha_{0,\mathrm{study}[j]} &\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2_{0,\mathrm{study}})
\text{, for study j = 1,} \dots \text{,J}
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\hat{\theta}_{ijkl}\) is the pairwise effect size, either the mean difference in REE or the log coefficient of variation ratio (calculated as PMOS vs control), for the \(j\textrm{th}\) study, conducted by the \(i\textrm{th}\) lab and \(\sigma^2_{ijkl}\) is the corresponding sampling error for that effect size estimate. The random intercepts for the \(i\textrm{th}\) lab, \(j\textrm{th}\) study are \(\alpha_{0,lab[i]}\) and \(\alpha_{0,study[j]}\) respectively each with standard deviation of \(\sigma^2_{0,lab[i]}\), \(\sigma^2_{0,study[j]}\). The parameter \(\beta_0\) represents the fixed effect estimate of the pairwise effect size i.e., the pooled estimate of the contrast between conditions. The priors for \(\beta_{0}\) in these models were set as default weakly regularising which is set on an intercept that results when internally centering all population-level predictors around zero to improve sampling efficiency and scaled to the expected response values using a \(\textrm{student-}t\) distribution; for the mean difference in REE this was \(\textrm{student-}t(3,\ 5.5,\ 50.2)\) and for the log coefficient of variance ratio this was \(\textrm{student-}t(3,\ -0.1,\ 2.5)\). The random effects were set similarly scaled to the expected response values but using a \(\textrm{half-student-}t\) distribution centred on zero. From these models we calculated the mean and 95% quantile intervals (i.e., ‘credible’ or ‘compatibility’ intervals) for the \(\beta_0\) (comparable to the \(\beta_1\) from the corresponding mean and standard deviation of REE arm-based models) for each effect size providing the most probable value of the parameter in addition to the range from 2.5% to 97.5% percentiles given our priors and data.
For reporting, posterior draws from the log coefficient-of-variation ratio were exponentiated before calculating the posterior mean and 95% quantile interval.


Additional sensitivity analyses
As noted in the section above, “Studies with possible reporting errors”, we opted to conduct analysis with and without the inclusion of four studies with possible reporting errors we could not resolve16–19. Thus the main models described above were run with and without these studies, the main results are presented without them and the sensitivity results with them are reported separately below.
As a further sensitivity analysis, given the inclusion of some studies with interventions in women with PMOS reporting REE at multiple timepoints such as mid- and post-intervention20–22 but lacking of control women without PMOS, we opted to also conduct sensitivity analysis excluding these and only examining their baseline results in addition to the cross-sectional studies. As such, the main models described above were run without the follow-up (i.e., mid- or post-intervention timepoints) from these studies and only using the baseline results in addition to other cross-sectional studies.
Lastly, given the role of body mass and, in particular, highly metabolically active tissue on REE we included models adjusted for these group level characteristics where studies reported them. These models were essentially extensions of the main models noted above for BMI and fat-free mass where each was modelled with its corresponding sampling error similarly to how the log mean REE was modelled in the models for standard deviation of REE i.e., the mean BMI or fat-free mass estimates were modelled as estimated with measurement error. We used the median values seen in the control conditions as the reference values i.e., BMI = 26.03 kg/\(\textrm{m}^2\) and fat-free mass = 48.8 kg. Because these models did not include condition-by-moderator interactions, the adjusted between-condition contrast corresponds directly to \(\beta_1\) and is invariant to the chosen reference value.

title: Supplementary Technical Analysis and Results
text:
Systematic Review
The searches were updated for the period January 2025 through September 2026. The global consensus adopting “Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome” (PMOS) was published only in June 2026, during the final months of the update23. For continuity with the original strategy and the terminology under which the historical literature was indexed, the updated strategy retained PCOS terminology. The update identified 69 records (PubMed, n = 38; Web of Science, n = 13; MEDLINE/EBSCO, n = 18). After removal of eight duplicate records, including records already captured by the original search, 61 records underwent title screening. Fifty-nine were excluded at title screening and the remaining two were excluded after abstract screening. No reports proceeded to full-text retrieval and no additional eligible studies were identified. The study set and all statistical analyses reported in this supplement were therefore unchanged.
The numbers in this section exclude the four studies previously noted with possible reporting issues that were unresolved. These studies are, however, summarised in full in the descriptive characteristics table in the online supplementary materials (see Descriptives Table), where some of the possible reporting errors can be seen in the standard deviations reported or calculated (e.g., the standard deviation calculated for body mass of women with PMOS in Saltamavros et al.17). The PRISMA flow diagram (Figure 1) includes all eligible studies, including the four with possible reporting errors, and the updated search.






Figure 1: Updated PRISMA 2020 flow diagram for the systematic review. The updated database search covered January 2025 through September 2026 and identified no additional eligible studies. A “report” may be a journal article, preprint, conference abstract, study register entry, clinical study report, dissertation, unpublished manuscript, government report, or another document providing relevant information. The website in the original-search pathway was a prior narrative review by members of the author group (https://macrofactorapp.com/pcos-bmr/) that identified two studies not found in the systematic database search.



Our systematic review identified 13 studies from 12 lab/research groups including 24 arms (Control arms = 9, PMOS arms = 15) and a total of 918 participants (Controls: minimum n = 9, median n = 29, maximum n = 54; PMOS: minimum n = 5, median n = 28, maximum n = 266). Descriptive characteristics of the arms and participants in these studies are reported fully in the online supplementary materials (see Descriptives Table).
Studies were carried out in multiple countries: Brazil (k = 3) ,and USA (k = 3 studies), Australia, Cameroon, Canada, Italy, Sweden, Turkey, UK (all k = 1 study). The four studies with noted reporting errors were carried out in Greece. A total of 11 studies used the Rotterdam criteria (or a modified version there of) for diagnosing PMOS20–22,24–31. One study used the 1990 National Institutes of Health criteria32, and two studies24,33 diagnosed PMOS via the presence of oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea alongside additional criteria including plasma androgen levels, hirsutism or polycystic ovaries on ultrasound scanning. All but one study32, which used doubly labelled water, measured REE using indirect calorimetry. The specific devices reported by these studies are included in the online supplementary materials (see Descriptives Table). We originally considered in our pre-registration that, given sufficient data, we would compare sub groups of women with PMOS who did and did not have accompanying insulin resistance. However, based on the metabolic health variables reported in studies with this information (see Descriptives Table) and, where available, considering primary criteria of either homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) \(\geq2.5\) or secondary criteria including fasting insulin \(>12\mu \textrm{U/mL}\) or fasting glucose \(\geq100\textrm{mg/dL}\), all groups of women with PMOS in the included studies would be considered to have insulin resistance. Mean age of women with PMOS in these studies ranged from 23 to 33 which was similar to the control women without PMOS ranging from 23 to 30. Across those studies where BMI was reported or it was possible to estimate the mean BMI of women with PMOS ranged from 26.4 to 39.9 was typically greater than women without PMOS which ranged 20.5 to 32.3.

title: Supplementary Technical Analysis and Results
text:
Mean REE Model Results
The main model for mean REE resulted in a posterior distribution for the contrast between control and PMOS conditions with a mean point estimate of 31 kcal/day with a 95% quantile interval ranging from -44 kcal/day to 113 kcal/day suggesting there is a 95% probability that the true difference lies between these values given our priors and the data from included studies. The corresponding conditional estimates for the control condition and PMOS condition respectively were 1442 kcal/day [95%QI:1332 kcal/day to 1553 kcal/day] and 1473 kcal/day [95%QI:1358 kcal/day to 1586 kcal/day]. These results, including the full visualisation of the posterior distribution and the conditional estimates by study, can be seen in Figure 2.








Figure 2: Posterior distribution, mean point estimates, and 95% quantile intervals for conditional estimates by study, global grand mean estimates by condition, and the contrast between conditions for mean resting energy expenditure of control women without PMOS and women with PMOS.

title: Supplementary Technical Analysis and Results
section: Standard Deviation of REE Model Results
text:
Standard Deviation of REE Model Results
The main model for the between participant standard deviation of REE resulted in a posterior distribution for the contrast ratio between control and PMOS conditions with a mean point estimate of 0.98 with a 95% quantile interval ranging from 0.71 to 1.32 suggesting there is a 95% probability that the true ratio of standard deviations lies between these values given our priors and the data from included studies. The corresponding conditional estimates for the standard deviations of the control condition and PMOS condition respectively were 238 kcal/day [95%QI:178 kcal/day to 312 kcal/day] and 229 kcal/day [95%QI:170 kcal/day to 301 kcal/day]. These results, including the full visualisation of the posterior distribution and the conditional estimates by study, can be seen in Figure 3.








Figure 3: Posterior distribution, variance point estimates, and 95% quantile intervals for conditional estimates by study, global grand variance estimates by condition, and the contrast ratio between conditions for the standard deviation of resting energy expenditure of control women without PMOS and women with PMOS.

title: Supplementary Technical Analysis and Results
text:
Sensitivity Analyses

Pairwise Models
For mean REE the pairwise model resulted in qualitatively similar inferences suggesting little difference between control and PMOS conditions with mean point estimate of 16 kcal/day with a 95% quantile interval ranging from -36 kcal/day to 70 kcal/day. This was similar for relative variability in REE, with the pairwise model resulting in a coefficient-of-variation ratio between the PMOS and control conditions with a mean point estimate of 0.92 and a 95% quantile interval ranging from 0.61 to 1.32.


Models including studies with possible reporting issues
For mean REE the model including the studies noted with possible reporting issues that were not resolved16–19 still resulted in qualitatively similar inferences suggesting little difference between control and PMOS conditions with mean point estimate of 15 kcal/day with a 95% quantile interval ranging from -67 kcal/day to 94 kcal/day. This was similar for the standard deviation of REE with the model including these studies resulting in a contrast ratio between the control and PMOS conditions with a mean point estimate of 1.26 and a 95% quantile interval ranging from 0.68 to 2.12.


Baseline REE Measurement Models
For mean REE the model which included only baseline REE measurements from studies involving interventions20–22, in addition to other cross-sectional studies, also resulted in qualitatively similar inferences suggesting little difference between control and PMOS conditions with mean point estimate of 32 kcal/day with a 95% quantile interval ranging from -45 kcal/day to 119 kcal/day. This was also the case for the standard deviation of REE with this model resulting in a contrast ratio between the control and PMOS conditions with a mean point estimate of 0.99 and a 95% quantile interval ranging from 0.71 to 1.35.


BMI and Fat-Free Mass Adjusted Models
For mean REE the model adjusted for BMI, also resulted in qualitatively similar inferences suggesting little difference between control and PMOS conditions with mean point estimate of 22 kcal/day with a 95% quantile interval ranging from -90 kcal/day to 145 kcal/day. This was also the case for the standard deviation of REE with this model resulting in a contrast ratio between the control and PMOS conditions with a mean point estimate of 0.93 and a 95% quantile interval ranging from 0.57 to 1.41. This was similar for fat-free mass adjusted models too showing little difference in mean REE between control and PMOS conditions with mean point estimate of -10 kcal/day with a 95% quantile interval ranging from -193 kcal/day to 167 kcal/day and a contrast ratio between the control and PMOS conditions with a mean point estimate of 0.87 and a 95% quantile interval ranging from 0.34 to 1.89.
